source_terms: Changing the distance of the light source changes the brightness of the background but not of the metal.

we expect the closer light to illuminate the background more brightly, but the brightness of the metal does not change because the brightness of direct reflection is not affected by the distance to the source
item.claim: Moving the source closer to a metal subject brightens the background and leaves the metal's brightness unchanged; moving it away darkens the background and again leaves the metal unchanged. This gives what looks like unlimited independent control over the relative brightness of metal and background from a single light. The source immediately qualifies it: sometimes it does and sometimes it does not, because the effective size of the light relative to the family of angles limits how far the light can travel before the metal is affected.

mechanism.text: The background is lit by diffuse reflection and therefore follows the inverse square law; the metal is lit by direct reflection, whose brightness equals that of the source regardless of distance. Two different laws act on the two surfaces from the same lamp.

scope.conditions: brightly polished metal against a diffusely reflecting background

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', section 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light'
item.question: Moving a soft box closer to a metal spatula on a white ground brightens the background and leaves the metal exactly as bright as it was. Why?
item.answer: Because two different laws are acting on the two surfaces from the same lamp. The background is lit by diffuse reflection, whose brightness follows the inverse square law, so it rises as the light comes closer. The metal is lit by direct reflection, whose brightness equals that of the source regardless of how far away the source is, so it does not change at all. The consequence is a near-independent control over the relative brightness of metal and background from a single light — the authors call it nearly infinite control and immediately hedge it, because the range is bounded by how much of the family of angles the source still covers as it recedes.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light', with its matched pair of spatula photographs at two light distances. The two underlying laws are chapter-3 material, already live Canon; what this chapter contributes is running them against each other in one scene.
confounders: assuming the metal must brighten too, since more light is falling on the whole set
attributing the effect to the light becoming effectively larger, which is a separate consequence of moving it
thinking the metal's constancy is an exposure artefact rather than a property of direct reflection

source_terms: Because the metal is a mirror, the camera is likely to reflect in the subject.
Although the camera is not visible in the subject, the hole in the light source is.
spending half a day lighting instead of spending half an hour at a computer makes absolutely no sense
item.claim: A camera placed square on to flat metal reflects in it. The source gives four remedies and is explicit about what each costs. A view camera or perspective-control lens is the best: the camera sits off-centre, outside the family of angles, with its back parallel to the subject so no perspective distortion is introduced, and the lens is shifted to re-centre the image — though a large shift may vignette the corners or reveal lens distortion, both minimised by working farther away with a longer lens. Shooting through a hole cut in the light source removes the camera's reflection but substitutes the hole's, which only works where the subject is irregular enough to camouflage it. Shooting at an angle and correcting in post always costs some image quality and requires composing loose enough to crop the trapezoid. Retouching the reflection out is not a lighting solution at all, but for some subjects it is so much cheaper than the lighting solutions that the source says it should not be forgotten, and it loses no quality.

mechanism.text: The camera lies inside the family of angles whenever it faces flat metal squarely; the remedies work either by moving the camera out of the family while keeping the image plane parallel, by concealing it inside the source, or by abandoning the geometric fix.

scope.conditions: flat metal that must appear centred and undistorted

caveats.text: the retouching recommendation is an economic judgement about a photographer's time, not an optical claim, and the source presents it as such

the source warns that lighting the area near the camera needs care in the hole-in-the-source arrangement: a light aimed at a reflector card can flare into the lens, and a light through a diffusion sheet can cast a shadow of the camera onto the sheet that then reflects visibly in the subject
the perspective-control lens note is partly technology-contingent — it names current manufacturers and compares their movement range with view cameras

item.rationale: SPEC-01 lets an entity declare `allowed_variation: {lighting: true, viewing_angle: true}` alongside the invariants that constitute its identity. This source supplies a physical basis for setting those two flags per surface rather than per product. A matte surface's recorded brightness is independent of viewing angle, so its appearance is close to an identity property. A polished one's is not: what a mirror-like product shows is an image of its surroundings, so the same physical object legitimately looks different from a different angle or in a different room, and its centre will show whatever is in front of it. Declaring viewing_angle variation permissible for a brushed-metal tin and impermissible for a matte carton is a different decision, and the source says why.

applicability.when: declaring which appearance changes count as identity violations for a product entity with reflective surfaces
applicability.limits: The source is describing what a physical camera records from a physical object. Whether a generator's variation across angles corresponds to this physics is unknown and is not claimed. The flags this informs are declarations of intent, not measurements. Treat as extractor inference: the source never discusses identity, invariants, or any specification format.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 6 'Metal', sections 'Keeping the Metal Bright', 'Keeping the Metal Dark' and 'The Elegant Compromise'
item.question: You are handed a brushed-steel flask and told it should read as a light mid-grey, sitting on a background that reads near-white, in one frame. Using only what this book gives you, how do you get both?
item.answer: Treat the two surfaces as reading different parts of the same source. The flask, being close to a pure direct reflector, responds only to whatever lies inside its family of angles; the background responds to the whole source through diffuse reflection. So one large soft source can serve both: the portion of it covering the family sets the flask's tone, and the whole of it sets the background's. Having more of the source inside the family makes the metal brighter; a source large enough that little of it falls inside makes the background brighter instead. Then use distance as the second control, since the background follows the inverse square law and the metal's direct reflection does not — moving the light closer lifts the background toward white while the flask holds its tone exactly. The book's phrase for this is the elegant compromise, and the claim worth taking from it is that the metal's tone is placeable at any step between black and white independently of the rest of the scene. The bound to watch is the lens: from a close viewpoint the family is wide and the source may only just fill it, in which case the light cannot be moved without the flask's edges going black.
item.support: Ch. 6, 'The Elegant Compromise' for the single-soft-box arrangement, 'Controlling the Effective Size of the Light' for both the distance control and the lens bound. The matched spatula frames show the tonal independence directly.
confounders: using two lights and balancing their power, which works but misses that one large source already gives the control
expecting the metal to brighten when the light comes closer
ignoring the lens constraint, which is what makes the control fail from a close viewpoint

source_terms: The precise tone of the metal is fully controllable, independently of the rest of the scene, and it can be any step between black and white that the photographer's creative judgment determines.

item.claim: The usual result is neither of the extremes but a compromise: light filling the family of angles to make the metal bright, plus light from other angles producing diffuse reflection from the background. Several arrangements produce the same picture and the source says the best is whichever suits the equipment on hand. The important claim is not that the compromise is the best picture but the control it demonstrates — the metal's tone can be placed at any step between black and white, independently of the rest of the scene. A single large soft box suffices, because the whole of it lights the background diffusely while only the part covering the family lights the metal; having more of the box inside the family makes the metal brighter, and a box large enough that little of it falls inside makes the background brighter instead.

mechanism.text: The two surfaces read different parts of the same source: the background responds to all of it through diffuse reflection, the metal only to the portion inside its family through direct reflection. Changing the fraction of the source inside the family therefore moves one without moving the other.

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 4 'Surface Appearances', section 'Complex Surfaces', the closing figure
item.question: The book says adding a three-dimensional object to a glossy flat surface both improves the picture and makes the lighting easier. Why does it help, and why does the chapter drop the idea immediately?
item.answer: It helps because the object's reflection in the surface is unambiguous evidence of gloss in a way that a featureless bright area is not: the reflection of a pair of eyeglasses in a polished lid tells the viewer the wood is glossy, and the authors say adding a secondary subject reveals the surface better than they are likely to render it alone. It makes the lighting easier for the same reason — the proof of the finish no longer has to be carried entirely by the shaped highlight. The chapter drops it because it had committed at the outset to two-dimensional and nearly two-dimensional subjects, and the authors say they cannot pursue the approach far without breaking that promise; three-dimensional subjects are the next chapter's business. So the claim is stated and demonstrated but deliberately not developed.

source_terms: One of the first, and most important, decisions that we have to make when we photograph a piece of metal is how bright we want it to be.
This is a critical step because it leads to two exactly opposite lighting set-ups.
the camera position is essential in any lighting diagram involving metal
item.claim: Before lighting metal, decide how bright it should appear. If bright, fill the family of angles that produces direct reflection; if dark, put the light anywhere else. Either way the first physical step is the same — find the family — but the two answers lead to exactly opposite arrangements, so the decision cannot be deferred. Because the family depends on where the camera is, a lighting diagram for metal is meaningless without the camera in it: the camera-to-subject relationship is at least as important as the subject.

mechanism.text: Polished metal is visible to the camera only through direct reflection, and direct reflection is available only from inside the family of angles, which is defined jointly by the camera position and the subject; so the light's position relative to that family fully determines the metal's tone.

scope.conditions: flat polished metal, extended by the source to metal of any shape

source_terms: changing your aperture also radically alters the 'depth of field' in your image
By throwing an area of your image out of focus you're effectively getting rid of detail. This causes your subject to really stand out
small f-number = small area of focus; big f-number = big area of focus
Landscape, and often portrait photography is generally less about capturing movement and far more about controlling your depth of field
item.claim: Aperture is presented as an attention control rather than a light control. A wide aperture (low f-number) gives a shallow depth of field, and Carroll's stated mechanism for why that helps is subtractive: throwing an area out of focus removes detail, and removing detail is what makes the subject stand out. A narrow aperture (high f-number) renders foreground through background sharp, which he uses to communicate the scale and detail of a landscape. His decision rule is to work backwards from the picture: if it is fundamentally about a moving subject, take control of the shutter; if it is about depth of field, take control of the aperture and let the camera settle the other.

mechanism.text: Out-of-focus regions carry less detail, and detail is what competes for attention. So restricting the zone of sharpness is a way of removing competitors rather than of emphasising the subject directly.

scope.conditions: lenses offering a usable range of apertures; a scene with depth

caveats.text: The narrow-aperture route carries a stated cost: the compensating shutter speed is slower, so a tripod or stable surface becomes necessary.
Carroll notes that on a camera with an optical viewfinder the effect is not visible before the exposure, only after. That is a 2014 statement about camera hardware.
"Small f-number = small area of focus" is a memory aid, not a description of the optics. Carroll offers no account of why aperture size governs depth of field.

source_stated_remedies: To achieve a shallow depth of field select 'Aperture Priority' and a wide open aperture (low f-number)
A narrow aperture (high f-number) causes everything from the foreground through to the background to be in focus
Work backwards. Ask yourself, 'what's my picture about?'

item.source_title: Michael Freeman, The Photographer's Eye: A Graphic Guide (Focal Press, 2013), Parts 4-10
item.question: Freeman is careful to distinguish "close" from "close-up". What is the difference in his terms, and what common assumption about equipment does he remove?
item.answer: Close-up, he says, is to do with magnification of small things. Close is a sense of being right up against the subject, shooting from nearer than most people would consider normal and possibly nearer than feels comfortable. The assumption he removes is that close means a wide-angle lens: he says close viewpoints do not always mean wide-angle lenses, and his own example was shot at close to normal, 48mm, with tight framing doing the work instead. He also separates the practical reasons for being close — no room to stand back, obstructions such as telegraph lines forcing an architectural photographer nearer — from the expressive one, and only the expressive one carries his claim about a personal and emotional connection.
item.support: CLOSE, converted-PDF page 110. The close/close-up distinction, the 48mm figure and the separation of practical from expressive reasons are all stated there.
confounders: the widespread assumption that a close viewpoint requires a wide-angle lens, which he contradicts with his own focal length
reading 'close' as macro or detail work, which is exactly the confusion he is guarding against
assuming the emotional connection comes from the lens rather than from the physical distance and the subject's eye level

item.source_title: Fil Hunter, Steven Biver & Paul Fuqua, Light: Science & Magic, 5th Edition (Focal Press), chapters beyond ch. 3
item.source_locator: Ch. 5 'Revealing Shape and Contour', section 'How Much Tonal Variation is Ideal?'
item.question: Why does the book say a simple cube can be lit with a black shadow and a white highlight while a product package usually cannot, and what does it refuse to give you?
item.answer: Because of where the detail is. A simple cube with no important detail on any of its sides can take the full range — the shadow can go black and the highlight white. A package that has to sell a product may have important detail on all three visible sides, and detail in either extreme would be lost, so the highlight must be only slightly brighter and the shadow only slightly darker than the third side. The depth clue is deliberately weakened in exchange for legibility. What the authors refuse to give is a number: they say they never specify lighting ratios in the book because the decision has to be based on the specific subject as well as personal taste. Their stated ideal — a highlight side, a shadow side and a side between — is offered as a standard for evaluating whatever lighting exists, not as a requirement good lighting must meet.
item.support: Ch. 5, 'How Much Tonal Variation is Ideal?', which states both the refusal and the package case in the same short section.
confounders: supplying a ratio anyway; the source's position is that it will not

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Considering the Practical in the Impractical — Easing Dissonance, Enhancing Totality: 'Typographic Strategies' (spine 6)
item.question: An expressive spread reads as a set of unrelated fragments. Samara's typographic remedy has a fallback for when the running text cannot take it. State the remedy and the fallback.
item.answer: The remedy is to apply the layout's macro-level compositional gestures to micro-scale elements such as text, at a smaller scale — which he says creates greater cohesion among disparate parts and alleviates the fractured or dissonant quality that often attends alternative compositional approaches. He notes that text at a legible point size will withstand a degree of manipulation without sacrifice. The fallback is for when that seems too challenging: treat subheadings and callouts or decks as a bridge between the macro and micro scales, so the gesture is carried by an intermediate element and the running text is left alone.

source_terms: I reject the procedures that I have seen, but I don't undervalue homework and thoroughness.
I hate researches where regular human beings are asked stupid questions. Obviously, you will get a stupid reply.

I don't want to hear stupid answers to stupid questions. I would much rather watch their body language. If they are chatting and not looking at the TV commercial after five seconds, we have lost them.
item.claim: Pandey distinguishes his position carefully: he rejects the research *procedures* he has seen, not homework or thoroughness, and states he has attended more research sessions than most creative people. His objection to the group discussion is that asking people to report a feeling about a pack produces a fabricated answer, and that the first fabrication then propagates round the group as agreement. In place of self-report he proposes direct behavioural observation: discard the headphones, watch body language, and treat a respondent who is chatting and not looking at the commercial after five seconds as lost.

mechanism.text: A respondent asked a question they have no genuine answer to will supply one to save face in front of a group, and subsequent respondents can then agree cheaply. The fabricated answer is then reported as a finding. Observed attention is not subject to that failure because it is not a report.

scope.conditions: Indian agency and client qualitative research as the author encountered it over a career from 1982; focus groups, one-way mirrors, dial meters. He explicitly extends the scepticism to neuro-response research ("Take it easy, folks") without having used it.

caveats.text: the five-second attention criterion is offered in passing and is not a validated threshold; the author proposes no way of checking it

his evidence is a list of his own successful campaigns that he says would have failed research. That is survivorship: campaigns that failed research AND would have failed in market are not counted, and neither are campaigns that passed research and succeeded
the dismissal of neuro-response research is asserted from no stated experience of it
the fabrication-and-propagation mechanism he describes is a real and independently recognised failure of group self-report; the mechanism is stronger than the evidence he gives for his conclusion

the source illustrates this position with a list of his own campaigns he says the procedures would have killed (sk_ppm_0011). That list is offered as illustration and the position does not depend on it: the fabrication-cascade mechanism stands or falls on its own, while the list is counterfactual about tests that were never run. No SPEC-03 relation is recorded between them, because none of the available relations expresses 'is illustrated by'

source_stated_remedies: observe attention and body language rather than collecting self-report

source_terms: Hard light comes from one direction and is typical of a spotlight or bright sunshine
Hard light causes anything in its path to become a highlight, while everything else remains dark
You can use the contrasts created by hard light to abstract or simplify your composition
The strong, decisive shadows that go hand in hand with hard light create depth and three-dimensionality
Shadows tell us the whole truth about light. They show us where it's coming from and how intense it is
The unevenness of hard light makes it tricky to work with, as you will lose detail somewhere
item.claim: Hard light — one direction, high intensity — does two separable things. Its contrast makes anything in its path a highlight and leaves everything else dark, which can be used deliberately to simplify a composition: the shadows become large masses that mask unnecessary detail, and attention is driven to the lit parts. Its shadows have razor-sharp edges, and those decisive shadows create depth and three-dimensionality by describing the angles of what they fall across. Carroll also states the reciprocal reading: shadows disclose where the light is coming from and how intense it is. The cost is unavoidable and he says so — hard light is uneven, so detail is lost somewhere, at one end of the range or the other.

mechanism.text: A single intense source divides the scene into lit and unlit rather than grading between them. The division does the simplifying, because unlit areas stop presenting detail; the sharpness of the boundary does the modelling, because an abrupt edge follows the form it crosses. The same division is what puts part of the range outside what can be recorded at once.

scope.conditions: direct sun, spotlights, or any single intense undiffused source

caveats.text: Both effects are argued through reproduced photographs which were not inspected. What is recorded here is the vocabulary and the stated mechanism, not the appearance of those images.
Carroll's remedy for the detail loss is exposure compensation, which chooses which end of the range to keep. It does not recover both. He is explicit that you will lose detail somewhere.

source_stated_remedies: Scroll towards the + to bring out detail in the shadows and to the − to bring out the detail in the highlights
use the contrasts created by hard light to abstract or simplify your composition

item.label: image_as_the_thing_actually_bought
item.description: A connected account of why image rather than product is what advertising sells: products in a category are often materially alike, consumers experience the name's associations as properties of the thing, so image becomes the differentiator, is built by consistency over decades, and defaults to quality for products consumed in public.

whole_system_claim.text: Where products are alike, what the consumer buys is the image, and the image is the advertiser's actual product. It is built only by projecting the same personality year after year, it defaults to an impression of quality for anything consumed visibly, and for parity products it is the only remaining ground of difference.

source_ref.section: Brand image; Make the product the hero

dependencies.nature: differentiating parity products by style rests on image being what is experienced

tradeoffs.nature: differentiate by advertising style, or drop comparison entirely and simply establish that the product is positively good; the source offers both for the same situation

conflicts.nature: The chapter holds that consumers buy the image rather than the product, and separately that the product itself should be made the hero and that there are no dull products. Both are stated firmly. The source does not say which governs when they point different ways.

evidence.system_level_uncertainty: Membership and the core claim are source-stated; the chapter treats image as a single connected subject across consecutive sections. The trade-off and the conflict are ours. The conflict is the more interesting of the two, because it sets two of the chapter's best-known prescriptions against each other.

provenance.section: Brand image; Make the product the hero; 'The positively good'

source_terms: Whenever you can, make the product itself the hero of your advertising.
there are no dull products, only dull writers
item.claim: The product itself should be made the hero of the advertising wherever possible. The source rejects the excuse that a product is too dull, holding that there are no dull products only dull writers, and reports never assigning a product to a writer not personally interested in it, because every bad campaign the author wrote was for a product that did not interest him.

caveats.text: the source notes that showing the product with utter simplicity takes courage, because the writer will be accused of not being creative

source_stated_remedies: make the product itself the hero
do not assign a product to a writer who is not interested in it

intra_source_relations.note: the source sets this against the cult of creativity

item.rationale: SPEC-01 already assigns each entity a role, with `hero` among the permitted values. This source supplies a rule for filling that field in commercial work: the customer occupies the hero role and the brand occupies a supporting one. A brief that marks the product or the brand as hero and also claims to be customer-centric is a detectable conflict between two fields we already hold.

applicability.when: assigning entity roles for a brand asset intended to persuade a customer
applicability.limits: SPEC-01's `hero` marks the primary visual subject of an asset, while this source's hero is the protagonist of a narrative the customer is living. Those are not the same thing, and a product can be the visual subject of a shot in which the customer is still the protagonist. The rule is usable as a check on the message; it must not be read as forbidding product-led imagery.

item.definition_in_origin_frame: Put the product itself at the centre of the advertising, shown with simplicity.

source_terms: so many products are no different from their competitors

all you can hope to do is explain their virtues more persuasively than your competitors, and to differentiate them by the style of your advertising. This is the 'added value' which advertising contributes
item.claim: Many products are not different from their competitors, because manufacturers share technology and use the same research to set colour, size, design and taste. For such parity products the only available moves are to explain their virtues more persuasively and to differentiate by the style of the advertising. The source calls this the added value advertising contributes.

mechanism.text: Shared technology and shared research methods converge products on the same attributes, leaving no product-level difference to advertise.

scope.conditions: product categories where competing products are materially alike

caveats.text: the author adds that he is not sufficiently puritanical to hate himself for it, marking the practice as one he expects to be criticised

source_stated_problems: so many products are no different from their competitors
source_stated_remedies: explain the product's virtues more persuasively than competitors do
differentiate by the style of the advertising

intra_source_relations.note: rests on image being what consumers experience
the positively good approach is offered as the alternative to claiming superiority

item.source_title: Henry Carroll, Read This If You Want to Take Great Photographs (Laurence King Publishing, 2014)
item.question: What does Carroll claim foreground interest does, and what does he say about how it gets into the picture?
item.answer: It offers the viewer a stepping stone into the image and heightens its sense of depth; without it, the eye feels too separated from the middle distance and background and the picture loses depth. The second half is the part that is easy to miss: it does not get into the picture by being noticed, it gets there by the photographer moving. He is explicit that the near material in his example is not there by chance, that the photographer positioned himself to make it an essential part of the composition, and that landscape photographers do not plonk a tripod anywhere — it is a case of exactly here, not around about here.
item.support: Foreground interest spread: foreground interest offers a stepping stone into your image and heightens its sense of depth; without it our eyes would feel too separated from the middle distance and background; the mud isn't there by chance, the photographer positioned himself.
confounders: describing it as a framing device; it is a depth and entry device
assuming it means anything in the foreground; Carroll requires it to be positioned for

item.definition_in_origin_frame: A product materially no different from its competitors, because manufacturers share technology and use the same research to set colour, size, design and taste.
The differentiation advertising style contributes to a product that is not itself different from its competitors.
